patient.name: Adaeze Okonkwo
patient.complaint: Right-sided facial droop that developed over the morning
background: 33 weeks pregnant with her first baby, uncomplicated so far
Cold sores in the past; a cold last week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with unilateral facial weakness: the forehead decides Bell's palsy (involved) versus stroke (spared), and the ear decides Bell's versus Ramsay Hunt (vesicles).

points: This morning: tea dribbles from the right side of her mouth.
Food tastes odd; her class sounds **painfully loud**.
Weakness built up over hours, not seconds.

steps.lead: A one-sided droop that evolved over hours in a well young woman with a cold sore history: think **LMN CN VII** palsy linked to HSV.
Adaeze's **pregnancy** is her biggest risk factor; last week's cold adds to it.

points: She **cannot wrinkle her right forehead** or raise the right eyebrow.
Right eye does not fully close; the eyeball rolls up (Bell's phenomenon).
Right nasolabial fold flattened; mouth droops on the right.
Arms and legs normal; other cranial nerves normal.

steps.lead: Every feature fits: forehead plus lower face, **lagophthalmos**, postauricular ache, taste change and **hyperacusis**.

steps.title: UMN or LMN facial weakness?
nodes: Ask her to raise both eyebrows
Forehead weak too → LMN (whole half of face)
Forehead spared → UMN (stroke until proven otherwise)
LMN + ear vesicles → Ramsay Hunt; LMN alone → Bell's
steps.caption: The eyebrow test is the single most important bedside step.

steps.q: Adaeze's whole right face, forehead included, is weak; limbs are normal. Which lesion fits?
steps.r: Forehead involvement means **LMN** on the same side. A cortical or capsular stroke would be **contralateral** and spare the forehead.

steps.lead: No forehead sparing, no limb weakness and only CN VII involved: no **red flags** for a central cause in Adaeze.

steps.title: Bell's palsy vs stroke vs Ramsay Hunt
head: Feature
Bell's palsy
Stroke (UMN)
Ramsay Hunt

steps.lead: Adaeze's right eye stays open and dries out, so her cornea is at risk of **exposure keratopathy**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical diagnosis), or MRI brain when the stem adds an atypical feature.

steps.q: Adaeze is worried and asks for a scan. What confirms her diagnosis?
steps.r: Bell's palsy is a **clinical diagnosis**. Typical LMN weakness with no red flags needs no imaging.

steps.lead: Adaeze's history and examination are the test: **no routine imaging**. Check ears, parotid and limbs to look for an alternative cause.

visual.title: House-Brackmann grade
visual.label: Adaeze IV
visual.caption: Grade IV: obvious weakness, eye will not close fully. Grade VI is complete paralysis.

steps.text: Grading the severity documents the baseline and flags complete paralysis.

points: Ear canals and drums normal; no parotid lump.
No other cranial nerve or limb signs.

steps.lead: If Adaeze had **atypical** features (slow progression, other cranial nerves, recurrence on the same side), **MRI brain** would exclude a central or structural cause.

steps.text: Do not order a CT head 'to be safe' for typical Bell's. CT is for suspected **stroke** (sudden, forehead-sparing, limb signs), not LMN palsy.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where the onset time decides: oral prednisolone within 72 hours, plus eye protection, and ENT referral if no recovery by 3 weeks.

visual.title: Hours since onset
visual.label: Adaeze 20 h
visual.caption: Adaeze is well inside the 72-hour window.

steps.q: Adaeze is 20 hours from onset. What is first-line treatment?
steps.r: **Oral prednisolone** within 72 hours. Antivirals alone are not first-line; thrombolysis is for ischaemic stroke.

steps.lead: Adaeze starts **prednisolone** today, 20 hours in (NICE: 50 mg for 10 days, or 60 mg for 5 days then taper). Pregnancy does not stop it.
Her paralysis is **incomplete** (grade IV), so no antiviral. Complete paralysis would make adding aciclovir or valaciclovir worth considering.
Adaeze's right eye cannot close: **lubricating drops** by day, **ointment** at night and **tape it shut** to sleep.

steps.title: Management pathway
nodes: Typical LMN palsy, onset ≤72h → oral prednisolone
No improvement at 3 weeks → urgent ENT referral
steps.caption: Red flags come first; the 72-hour clock decides steroids.

steps.lead: Had Adaeze's forehead been spared or an arm weak, this would be a **stroke** call, not a steroid prescription.
Adaeze is safety-netted: if there is **no improvement by 3 weeks**, she needs an **urgent ENT** referral.
Adaeze's plan follows **NICE CKS**: steroid within 72h, eye care, review, and referral if recovery fails.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the forehead is involved in Bell's but spared in stroke, or which branch explains hyperacusis or taste loss.

steps.lead: Adaeze's cold sore virus, **HSV-1**, is thought to reactivate and swell her facial nerve inside its tight bony canal.

steps.title: From virus to droop
nodes: HSV-1 reactivation in the facial nerve
Narrow bony facial canal: nowhere to expand
Compression and ischaemia of the nerve
LMN weakness of the whole ipsilateral face

steps.lead: The squeeze is on the nerve itself, below the nucleus, so **every** muscle on Adaeze's right side, forehead included, is weak.
A stroke would spare Adaeze's forehead because each side of the upper face gets **bilateral cortical** supply.

steps.q: Why are loud sounds painful for Adaeze?
steps.r: The **nerve to stapedius** (CN VII) damps loud sound. Tensor tympani is CN V3; chorda tympani is taste.

steps.lead: Adaeze's **hyperacusis** is the stapedius branch; her odd taste is the **chorda tympani** (anterior 2/3 of the tongue).

visual.title: Adaeze's recovery
visual.caption: Improving by 3 weeks, so no ENT referral needed; fully recovered by 4 months.

steps.lead: Adaeze recovers over weeks to months as the inflammation settles and the nerve is no longer compressed.

mcq.q: Which cranial nerve is affected in Bell's palsy?
mcq.r: Bell's palsy is an LMN lesion of the **facial nerve (CN VII)**.

mcq.q: Which is the strongest risk factor for Bell's palsy?
mcq.r: **Pregnancy** is the strongest; diabetes and recent viral illness also increase risk.

mcq.q: Which sign best separates Bell's palsy from a stroke?
mcq.r: Bell's (LMN) weakens the forehead; stroke (UMN) **spares** it. The lower-face signs occur in both.

mcq.q: Which eye complication does Bell's palsy cause?
mcq.r: **Lagophthalmos** dries the cornea, causing exposure keratopathy and ulceration.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing Bell's palsy?
mcq.r: It is a **clinical diagnosis**; no routine imaging.

mcq.q: When is MRI brain indicated in suspected Bell's palsy?
mcq.r: **Atypical features** prompt MRI to exclude central or structural causes.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment and when must it start?

mcq.r: No improvement after **3 weeks** means **urgent ENT** referral.

mcq.q: Why does a stroke spare the forehead?
o: Bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face
Separate facial nerve trunk to the forehead
mcq.r: The upper face has **bilateral cortical** supply, so one-sided UMN lesions spare it.

mcq.q: Which branch explains altered taste in Bell's palsy?
mcq.r: The **chorda tympani** carries taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

ear canal and pinna look normal

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Isolated acute LMN facial palsy with postauricular pain: **Bell's palsy**.

elim: Stroke spares the forehead and is sudden, with other deficits.

steps.x: **A. Bell's palsy.** Rule: forehead involved + normal ear + nothing else = Bell's.

o: Eye care and review in 3 weeks only

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

Antiviral alone is not first-line; the steroid is the key drug.
Forehead involved, no limb signs: not a stroke.

Facial nerve compression in the facial canal

practice.stem: A 52 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 1 day history of left-sided facial weakness. He had pain behind his left ear 2 days ago. practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute LMN facial palsy (forehead involved) with a postauricular prodrome in a diabetic is Bell's palsy. Ramsay Hunt needs ear vesicles; stroke spares the forehead.

steps.x: Diagnosis: UMN vs LMN, then look for vesicles.
Diabetes is a risk factor; postauricular pain prodrome; forehead weak = LMN; ear clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute isolated LMN CN VII palsy: **Bell's palsy**.

elim: Acoustic neuroma is slow, with hearing loss and tinnitus.
Stroke would spare the forehead.
Lyme needs tick exposure or a rash.
Ramsay Hunt needs vesicles; there are none.

steps.x: **B. Bell's palsy.** Diabetes raises risk; a raised glucose does not make it a stroke.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has woken with a drooping right side of her mouth. Over the morning she has found that food tastes strange and loud noises are uncomfortable. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. She has no limb weakness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Inability to raise the right eyebrow
Vesicles in the right ear canal
practice.e: Pregnancy, altered taste and hyperacusis point to Bell's palsy, an LMN lesion, so the right forehead is weak too. Vesicles would mean Ramsay Hunt.

steps.x: A finding question: name the diagnosis, then its key sign.
Pregnancy (strongest risk factor), chorda tympani and stapedius involvement: Bell's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bell's is LMN, so the **forehead** on the same side is weak.

elim: Arm drift implies a central lesion; limbs are normal.
Hyperreflexia is an UMN sign.
The droop is on the right, the same side as the lesion.
Ear vesicles would make it Ramsay Hunt, not expected here.

steps.x: **C. Inability to raise the right eyebrow.** Bell's = whole half of the face, forehead included.

practice.stem: A 41 year old man was diagnosed with Bell's palsy 5 days ago. He has not been using any eye treatment. He now has a gritty, red, watery right eye. He cannot fully close his right eyelid. His visual acuity is slightly reduced in the right eye. His temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 74 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his eye symptoms?
practice.e: Lagophthalmos lets the tear film evaporate and dries the cornea: exposure keratopathy, which can progress to ulceration. Glaucoma gives a painful red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and headache.

steps.x: A cause question: link the eye to the palsy.

clues: not been using any eye treatment
cannot fully close his right eyelid
steps.x: **Lagophthalmos** with no protection; gritty eye = surface (corneal) problem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Corneal drying: **exposure keratopathy**.

elim: Glaucoma: severe pain, haloes, fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Uveitis: photophobia and ciliary flush, not linked to lid closure.
CRVO causes painless visual loss, not grittiness.
Endophthalmitis follows surgery or trauma.

steps.x: **E. Exposure keratopathy.** Prevent with drops, night ointment and taping.

practice.q: Which feature of her history most increases her risk of this condition?
practice.e: Pregnancy is the strongest risk factor for Bell's palsy. Diabetes and recent viral illness also raise risk; the anaemia, asthma and migraine do not.

steps.x: A risk factor question about Bell's palsy.
Acute isolated LMN palsy = Bell's; she is pregnant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

The low Hb and ferritin are distractors.

steps.x: **D. Pregnancy.** Also: diabetes and recent viral illness.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has a 1 day history of right-sided facial weakness affecting his forehead and mouth. He had an ache behind his right ear the day before. He has no limb weakness, and his ears look normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which additional symptom is he most likely to report?
o: Reduced taste on the front of the tongue
practice.e: In Bell's palsy the chorda tympani is involved, so taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is altered. Numbness is CN V, and diplopia, dysphagia and hoarseness suggest other cranial nerves (a red flag).

steps.x: A symptom question: which CN VII function is lost?
LMN palsy, postauricular prodrome, no vesicles: Bell's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CN VII also carries **taste** via the chorda tympani.

elim: Diplopia means CN III, IV or VI: a red flag.
Dysphagia means CN IX/X involvement.
Hoarseness is CN X.
Facial sensation is CN V, not VII.

steps.x: **E. Reduced taste on the front of the tongue.** Other CN involvement = think central.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 2 day history of left-sided facial weakness. She cannot wrinkle her left forehead, close her left eye or smile on the left. NMJ disease is fatigable and usually bilateral.
A right cortical lesion spares the forehead.
The right parotid would affect the right side, and grows slowly.

practice.stem: A 56 year old man was told he had Bell's palsy 6 weeks ago. His right facial weakness has slowly worsened since, and he now has twitching of the right cheek. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. The ear canal is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Gradual progression and twitching are atypical for Bell's palsy, so MRI brain is needed to exclude a structural or central cause (and he needs ENT review). CT is the acute stroke test.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has a 1 day history of right-sided facial weakness involving her forehead, with no other neurological signs. A CT head was performed in the emergency department because she was worried. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Acute infarct in the left internal capsule
practice.e: This is typical Bell's palsy, which is a clinical diagnosis with a normal brain scan, which is why imaging is not routine. An infarct would spare the forehead.

A CPA mass gives gradual onset with hearing loss.

No head injury is described.

steps.x: **D. No abnormality.** That is why no routine imaging is needed.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has started oral prednisolone for Bell's palsy diagnosed yesterday. He cannot fully close his right eye, and it feels dry. He sleeps alone and asks how to protect his eye. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman was diagnosed with Bell's palsy 3 weeks ago and completed a course of oral prednisolone. Her right facial weakness has not improved at all. She has no new neurological symptoms. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has a 2 day history of left-sided LMN facial weakness with no ear vesicles. He reports that ordinary sounds, such as doors closing, are painfully loud in his left ear. Hearing tests are normal. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.

glossary.Bell's palsy: Acute, one-sided lower motor neurone weakness of the facial nerve with no other cause found.
glossary.CN VII: The facial nerve: moves the face and carries taste, tear, saliva and stapedius fibres.
glossary.facial nerve: Cranial nerve VII; supplies the muscles of facial expression.
glossary.LMN: Lower motor neurone: from the brainstem nucleus to the muscle; lesions weaken the whole half of the face.
glossary.UMN: Upper motor neurone: from cortex to brainstem; a facial UMN lesion spares the forehead.
glossary.lower motor neurone: The nerve from the brainstem nucleus to muscle; damage weakens the entire ipsilateral face.
glossary.HSV: Herpes simplex virus; HSV-1 reactivation is the leading theory for Bell's palsy.
glossary.HSV-1: Herpes simplex virus type 1, the cold sore virus, thought to cause Bell's palsy.
glossary.VZV: Varicella zoster virus, the chickenpox and shingles virus; it causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
glossary.Ramsay Hunt syndrome: Facial nerve palsy from VZV reactivation, with severe ear pain and vesicles in or around the ear.
glossary.lagophthalmos: Inability to fully close the eyelids.
glossary.Bell's phenomenon: The eyeball rolls upward when the patient tries to close the eye.
glossary.nasolabial fold: The skin crease running from the side of the nose to the corner of the mouth.
glossary.prodrome: Early symptoms before the main illness appears.
glossary.hyperacusis: Ordinary sounds feel abnormally or painfully loud.
glossary.stapedius: Tiny middle-ear muscle, supplied by CN VII, that damps loud sounds.
glossary.chorda tympani: Branch of CN VII carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
glossary.exposure keratopathy: Damage to the cornea from drying when the eye does not close.
glossary.corneal ulceration: A break in the corneal surface that can threaten vision.
glossary.tear film: The thin fluid layer that keeps the cornea moist.
glossary.facial canal: The narrow bony tunnel in the temporal bone through which the facial nerve runs.
glossary.forehead sparing: Preserved forehead movement despite lower-face weakness; a sign of an UMN (central) lesion.
glossary.bilateral cortical innervation: Both hemispheres supply the upper face, so a one-sided cortical lesion spares the forehead.
glossary.prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid; first-line in Bell's palsy if started within 72 hours.
glossary.valaciclovir: Oral prodrug of aciclovir with better absorption.
glossary.House-Brackmann: Grading scale for facial nerve function, from I (normal) to VI (complete paralysis).
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; used in atypical cases to exclude central or structural lesions.
glossary.NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: UK primary care guidance.
glossary.Lyme disease: Tick-borne Borrelia infection that can cause facial palsy, sometimes bilateral.
glossary.acoustic neuroma: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve causing hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance.
glossary.parotid: Salivary gland in front of the ear; the facial nerve runs through it.
